title: Ask for God's Word, Then Refuse It
summary: The frightened survivors ask Jeremiah to pray for guidance and solemnly swear to obey whatever God says, pleasant or unpleasant. After ten days the answer comes: stay in the land and God will build and plant them, but go to Egypt and the sword and famine they fear will follow them there. Jeremiah ends by warning that they have already deceived themselves, because they asked for a word they had no intention of keeping.
story: After Gedaliah's murder (chapter 41), the survivors are camped near Bethlehem, already pointed toward Egypt. This chapter is the moment of decision. For the first time in a long while, the people come to Jeremiah on their own and ask him to seek God's will, and they promise to obey it. The scene looks like repentance. The answer God gives is gracious: the judgment has fallen, and now he offers to plant rather than uproot. But the chapter's final verses reveal that the question was never open. This is the last great choice set before Judah in the book, and chapter 43 shows which way they went.
historical:
The survivors had good reason to fear. Babylon had appointed Gedaliah, and his murder, along with the killing of Babylonian soldiers at Mizpah (41:3), would look like rebellion. Babylon had already shown what it did to rebels. Egypt, by contrast, was the traditional refuge for people fleeing trouble in Canaan, and Judah's leaders had looked to Pharaoh for help throughout the final years of the kingdom (37:5-7). Egyptian records and later papyri show that people from Judah and the wider Levant lived in Egypt in this period, some as soldiers and settlers.

Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah in verse 1 appears in 43:2 as Azariah son of Hoshaiah. He may be the same man known by two names, or one of the names may have been altered in copying; ancient manuscripts and translations differ here. Either way, he and Johanan lead the group. Jeremiah's promise that the king of Babylon would show compassion (verse 12) matches the lenient treatment Babylon had shown to Jeremiah and to those who cooperated with Gedaliah.
cultural:
Asking a prophet to inquire of God on behalf of the community was a recognized practice in Israel, often for a king before battle or in a crisis (1 Kings 22:5, 2 Kings 22:13). The people's oath in verses 5 and 6 calls God as a witness against them if they fail to act on his word, a solemn form of self-cursing well known in the ancient world. To break such an oath was to invite God's judgment on oneself.

The people's picture of Egypt (verse 14) is revealing: a place where they would not see war, hear the ram's horn (the shofar, blown to sound the alarm of battle), or go hungry for bread. Egypt, with the Nile's reliable floods, was famous as a land of food even when Canaan suffered drought, which is why Abraham and Jacob's family went there in famine (Genesis 12:10, 46:3-4). For Israel, however, Egypt was also the land of slavery, and Deuteronomy 17:16 had warned that the king must not lead the people back there.
literary: The chapter is built as a formal consultation with an unexpected ending. The request (verses 1 to 3), Jeremiah's promise (verse 4), and the people's oath (verses 5 and 6) set up the expectation of obedience. After ten days, the answer is given in two balanced halves: the promise if they stay (verses 10 to 12) and the warning if they go (verses 13 to 18). The promise uses the language of Jeremiah's call in 1:10, building and planting rather than tearing down and uprooting, signaling that the time of judgment could now turn to restoration. The warning turns their hopes inside out: the sword and famine they fear will follow them into the very land they think is safe. Verses 19 to 22 then close with Jeremiah's accusation, which reveals what he evidently already knew about their hearts.

outline.t: The remnant asks Jeremiah to pray for guidance
Jeremiah agrees, and the people swear to obey
God's answer: stay, and I will build and plant you
The warning: go to Egypt, and disaster will follow

doctrines.note: God answers the request clearly after ten days of waiting. The difficulty is not hearing God's word but receiving it. The chapter shows that asking for guidance with a mind already made up is a form of self-deception (verse 20).

God invites the remnant to trust him rather than their own reading of the danger: “Do not be afraid of the king of Babylon, whom you now fear” (verse 11). Faith here means staying where God says, even when fleeing looks safer.

After judgment, God offers restoration: “I will build you up and not tear you down; I will plant you and not uproot you” (verse 10). His mercy is ready even for the survivors of a disaster they brought on themselves.

words.note: Nacham, here to relent or change course. God says he will relent of the disaster he has brought (verse 10). The word does not mean God admits a mistake; it describes his readiness to turn from judgment to mercy when the situation calls for it, as Jeremiah 18:7-10 explains.

Gur, to sojourn, to live somewhere as a resident alien without full rights. It is used of Abraham in Canaan and of Israel in Egypt (Genesis 47:4). The people plan to go and sojourn in Egypt (verses 15 and 17), becoming again what their ancestors were before the exodus.

Shama, to hear, which in this chapter means to obey. The people promise to hear the voice of the LORD (verse 6), and Jeremiah says they have not heard it (verse 21). In Hebrew thought, hearing that does not lead to action is not really hearing.

Taah, to go astray or wander, and in the form used here, to lead astray or deceive. Jeremiah tells them they have led themselves astray (verse 20). The danger was not a false prophet but their own desire, dressed up as a request for guidance.

christ: The chapter sets before the remnant a choice between trusting God where they are and fleeing to a place of apparent safety. Jesus spoke of that same choice when he taught that whoever tries to save their life will lose it and whoever loses it for his sake will find it, and he himself refused to flee from Jerusalem when danger came. The New Testament doesn't quote this chapter, so the link is thematic. It shows a people who asked God for direction but would accept only one answer, and the gospel presents Jesus as the one who prayed in Gethsemane that not his will but his Father's would be done, the obedience this remnant refused.

hard.q: Why was going to Egypt wrong? Wasn't it sensible to flee from a dangerous empire?
hard.a: From a purely strategic point of view, fleeing looked prudent, and the fear was reasonable after the killing of Babylonian soldiers. The text doesn't claim Egypt was evil in itself; Abraham and Jacob's family had gone there in famine, and Jesus would later be taken there as an infant. The issue is that God had spoken a specific word for this moment, and the people had asked for it and sworn to obey it. Going was disobedience to a direct command, not simply a bad tactical choice. There is also a theological background: Egypt was the house of slavery from which God had redeemed Israel, and Deuteronomy 17:16 warned against returning. Jeremiah's point is that the only real safety is in obedience, and that no place is safe from the consequences of refusing God.

questions: The people promised to obey God's word whether it was pleasant or unpleasant, then refused it when it came. Have you ever asked for guidance while privately hoping for one particular answer?
God promised to build and plant the people in the very land where disaster had struck. What might it mean to trust God to rebuild where things have fallen apart, rather than running away?
The remnant believed Egypt would be free of war and hunger. What places or plans do people treat as refuges from trouble, and what does this chapter say about them?
